*	Kingdom Fungi includes edible mushrooms such as Agaricus bisporus (common mushroom) and Agaricus campestris (field mushroom) as well as a variety of moulds such as Mucor mucedo and Penicillium species. Their cells are described as eukaryotic.
Bacteria belong to the kingdom Prokaryotae whose cells are described as prokaryotic.
a	State two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. 	(2 marks)

Early classification systems, such as that used by Carl Linnaeus, divided all organisms into two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia. Bacteria, fungi, protozoans and algae were all included in the Plantae.

Since the middle of the twentieth century various scientists have suggested more appropriate divisions of organisms, such as the 'five-kingdom' system: Prokaryotae, Protoctista (Protista), Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
b	Suggest two reasons why it is inappropriate to classify fungi in the Plantae.
Seaweeds are algae which are autotrophic. They contain eukaryotic cells, with cellulose cell walls, which are aggregated into tissues showing limited differentiation.
c	Algae are now classified as the Protoctista instead of the Plantae, but not all scientists agree with this.
i	Suggest one reason why some scientists might think it is more appropriate to include the algae in the Plantae. 			(1 mark)
ii	Suggest one reason why many scientists think it is not appropriate to include algae in the Plantae. 							(1 mark)
CCEA GCE (AS) Biology Module 2 Jan 2012 Q4a, d, e
a	Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane / true nucleus, but eukaryotic cells do. 														1m
Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound organelles but eukaryotic cells do.															1m
Cell walls of fungi are not made of cellulose.						1m
c	i	Both algae and plants are autotrophic / carry out photosynthesis / have cellulose cell walls.										1m
ii	Plants have well differentiated tissues.						1m

*	Read the article below and answer the questions.

Aristotle was a Greek philosopher in the 4th century BC. He classified organisms into two groups, plants and animals. He further classified animals according to whether they had blood and whether they lived on land or in water. His system was used until the 17th century, when voyages of exploration brought new plants and animals to Europeans. People found that Aristotle's system failed to classify many of the new plants and animals.

In the 18th century, Carolus Linnaeus, a Swedish biologist, developed a new classification system. He classified organisms into two kingdoms, plants and animals. Then he divided each kingdom into smaller groups at different levels based on their structural similarities.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, better microscopes were developed. Biologists were able to observe organisms in greater detail and used new criteria to classify organisms. New kingdoms were established based on new evidence.
